## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ambasakkarapetavatthu* (Pv 36) is a narrative poem in the *Mahāvagga* of the *Petavatthu* (PTS pp. 45–57) [Marino 2017; SuttaCentral]. Framed around the central question of how one escapes the path leading to hell, the narrative depicts the titular ruler, King Ambasakkhara, alongside a *yakkha-peta* (yakṣa ghost) witnessing the prolonged public torture of a criminal who is bound or impaled on a stake [Marino 2017; SuttaCentral]. Prompted by the criminal's agony and dread of hellish torment, the ghost warns the king that impalement on a stake is vastly preferable to the terrors of hell, cautioning Ambasakkhara that he too remains at risk of such an excruciating fate [Marino 2017].

Text reuse data compiled by DharmaNexus records extensive verbatim reuse between the text and the *Petavatthu-aṭṭhakathā*, alongside shared passages across several other *Petavatthu* and *Vimānavatthu* poems—such as the *Maṭṭhakuṇḍalīpetavatthu* (Pv 17), *Maṭṭhakuṇḍalīvimānavatthu* (Vv 83), *Nandakapetavatthu* (Pv 38), and *Serīsakapetavatthu* (Pv 37)—as well as the *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā* and *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Machine alignments generated by DharmaNexus further link portions of the text to Buddhist literature in other languages, including Tibetan translations of the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Bimbisārapratyudgamana-mahāsūtra*, the Sanskrit *Ajitasenavyākaraṇa*, and a Chinese translation of the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* (T 120), although these cross-language matches represent algorithmic text reuse rather than established canonical parallels [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral registers five translations in five modern languages [SuttaCentral].
